title: Stop Leaking API Keys By Accident
subtitle: A fast checklist for handling secrets safely in any stack.

slides.heading: The mistake almost every dev makes
points: Committing a .env file to git
Secrets stay in history even after deleting
Public repo scanners find keys in minutes
slides.alt: A slide explaining that committing a .env file leaks secrets even after you delete it, because git history keeps it.

slides.heading: Ignore env files before committing
slides.alt: A code slide showing a .gitignore snippet that excludes .env, .env.local, and .env.*.local files.

slides.heading: Load secrets with process.env
slides.code:
const key = process.env.API_KEY;
if (!key) throw new Error('No key');
slides.alt: A code slide showing how to read an API key from process.env and fail fast if it is missing.

slides.heading: Client code is never private
points: Anything shipped to the browser is public
Only prefix truly public vars (e.g. NEXT_PUBLIC_)
Keep real secret keys server-side only
slides.alt: A slide warning that any variable bundled into frontend JavaScript is visible to anyone, so secrets must stay server-side.

slides.heading: If a key leaks, rotate fast
points: Revoke the old key immediately
Generate a fresh one from the provider
Update every environment that used the old key
slides.alt: A slide listing the steps to take right after an API key leaks: revoke, regenerate, and update everywhere it was used.

slides.heading: Production needs a secret manager
points: Use your host's built-in secret storage
Vercel, Render, and Railway all support it
Avoid plain text config files on servers
slides.alt: A slide recommending built-in secret managers on hosts like Vercel, Render, and Railway instead of plain text config files.

slides.heading: Save this before your next push
points: Save it before your next commit
Send it to a teammate who needs it
slides.alt: A closing slide encouraging viewers to save this checklist before their next git push and share it with a teammate.

title: Add Stripe checkout in one afternoon
subtitle: The real steps from product to verified payment

slides.heading: The Goal
points: One button triggers real payment
Stripe hosts the checkout page
No backend payment form needed
slides.alt: A slide stating the goal: a button that triggers a real payment without building a custom payment form.

slides.heading: Create A Product
points: Add product and price in dashboard
Copy the price ID it generates
This ID goes in your code
slides.alt: A slide showing how to create a product and price in the Stripe dashboard and copy its price ID.

slides.heading: Install Stripe
slides.alt: A terminal command installing the Stripe Node package with npm install stripe.

slides.heading: Create Checkout Session
slides.alt: Server code creating a Stripe checkout session with payment mode, a line item, and success and cancel URLs.

slides.heading: Redirect The Customer
points: Send them to session.url
Stripe collects card details securely
You never touch raw card numbers
slides.alt: A slide explaining to redirect the customer to the checkout session URL returned by Stripe.

slides.heading: Verify With Webhook
points: Listen for checkout.session.completed event
Grant access only after that event
Never trust the success redirect alone
slides.alt: A slide warning to verify payment through a Stripe webhook event, not the success redirect alone.

slides.heading: Test Before Going Live
points: Use Stripe test mode keys
Trigger events with Stripe CLI
Switch keys when going live
slides.alt: A slide recommending testing with Stripe test mode keys and the Stripe CLI before switching to live keys.

takeaway: One checkout session. Real payments, no custom form.
question: What payment step always trips you up?
caption:
Add Stripe checkout in one afternoon
No backend payment page needed, just one API call.
What payment step always trips you up?
Comment STRIPE and I'll send you the full guide 👇
dm_guide: Install: npm install stripe. 1) In the Stripe dashboard, create a Product and Price, copy the price ID. 2) Server: const session = await stripe.checkout.sessions.create({mode:'payment', line_items:[{price:'price_xxx', quantity:1}], success_url, cancel_url}); then redirect to session.url. 3) Verify payment server-side: run `stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhook` (Stripe CLI), check event.type === 'checkout.session.completed' before granting access. Full docs: https://docs.stripe.com/checkout/quickstart

caption:
How to write a freelance proposal that wins the job
Most proposals lose before the client finishes reading them.
Fix the structure, not your resume.
What's the last line of your best proposal? 👇
dm_guide: Proposal structure that gets replies: 1) Restate their exact problem in one line, skip your bio entirely. 2) Give a price range anchored to scope, not hours worked. 3) End with one next step only, something like "Free for a 15 min call Tuesday or Wednesday?" Keep the whole thing to one page covering just problem, plan, price. Send it within 24 hours of talking to them. Skip generic templates, rewrite the opening line for every client so it names their actual problem.
question: What's the last line of your best proposal?

slides.heading: The proposal that gets ignored
slides.alt: A code block shows a generic freelance proposal opening with the developer's bio and ending with let me know your thoughts.
slides.code:
Hi, I'm a full-stack dev with
5 years experience. I'd love
to help with your project.

slides.heading: The proposal that gets replies
slides.alt: A code block shows a rewritten proposal naming the client's specific problem, a price range, and a request for a short call.
slides.code:
Your [specific problem] costs
you time every week. I'll fix
it in 1 week, $800-1200.
Free for a 15 min call Tue?

slides.heading: Open with their problem
points: Restate their exact goal in one line
Skip your bio entirely
Prove you listened before you pitch
slides.alt: Slide explaining to open a proposal by restating the client's exact problem instead of a personal bio.

slides.heading: Price as a range
points: Give a range, not one number
Anchor the high number first
Tie it to scope, not hours
slides.alt: Slide showing how to present a price as a scope-based range instead of a single hourly rate.

slides.heading: One clear next step
points: Ask for a 15 minute call
Never end with let me know
Make saying yes effortless
slides.alt: Slide recommending every proposal end with a request for a short call instead of an open ended question.

slides.heading: Keep it to one page
points: Cut anything they can Google
Three sections only: problem, plan, price
Long proposals get skimmed, not read
slides.alt: Slide advising freelance proposals stay one page covering only the problem, the plan, and the price.

slides.heading: Send within 24 hours
points: Speed signals you want the work
Late replies lose to faster ones
A template saves you the time
slides.alt: Slide noting that sending a proposal within 24 hours wins more freelance work than a slower, polished one.
